en: The *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyāna-sūtra* on Manifesting Transgressions:
Dwelling in the Great Treasury of Wisdom, it resides within the realm of sentient beings; it is likened to a priceless wish-fulfilling jewel.
Within the meditative contemplation of all phenomena, this is the master of the practice of great correspondence;
if one attains the most supreme method of correspondence, there is none equal to one in yoga.
Whether appearing as Brahmā, Śakra, or the Four Heavenly Kings, or manifesting as hosts of great seers from non-Buddhist paths.
Or again, manifesting transformations in the form of a Buddha-body, appearing everywhere throughout the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
or appearing as an eight-armed Bodhisattva and the like, or appearing with three eyes and blazing flames—
those who have attained mastery in yoga can manifest all manner of worldly bodies.
Capable of donning the great armor of compassion, Holding joy as his bow,
he skillfully shoots the arrows of wisdom and the sublime Dharma; He possesses great power within the subtle [state] of ignorance,
is able to act with swift speed, And wields the firm iron mallet of wisdom.
He shatters the shell of ignorance and afflictions, Completely pulverizing them until not a trace remains;
The most honored among all powerful heroes, Wielding a vajra-tipped mace of blazing flames,
Manifests a terrifying vajra body For the sake of subduing sentient beings.
Or again, he may manifest a body of true golden color, adorned with the radiance of various jewels;
for the sake of rescuing impoverished sentient beings, he manifests the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
If one practices subtle and manifold wholesome deeds, one will be able to experience the fruits of various supreme joys.
If one can instruct others according to the Dharma, regarding them with impartiality and without partial views;
if one provides various kinds of delicious food and drink to those who suffer from hunger, thirst, and the heat of affliction;
and if, when they are in the midst of illness and suffering, one manifests as a King of Physicians capable of providing healing—
For those who are blind, ignorant, and without wisdom, you act as the eye of pure insight;
able to travel through ten billion Buddha-fields, you tame sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness.
You do not suffer from toil nor do you speak of weariness, for you have long practiced compassion until it has become your very essence.
Through the sovereign power of all the bases of miraculous ability, you have realized yoga and reached the further shore;
disregarding likes and dislikes, you act with compassion at all times,
always able to cross over those most wicked places of flattery and strife, never for even a moment giving rise to a mind of indifference.
Your countenance and deportment are as radiant as the sun and moon; Your light issues forth in response to thought, appearing with swift velocity like a flash of lightning.
It illuminates billions of Buddha-fields, taming immeasurable classes of sentient beings, Purifying them all equally and simultaneously.
Universally able to manifest the bodies of all Buddhas, They appear entirely within a single thought-moment.

The triple world is as deep and vast as the great ocean; Pervadingly they filter out all sentient beings, Skillfully casting the net of the sublime Dharma, To lead them into the city of the Buddha-Dharma’s discipline.
By the power of that net of subduing, you are able to rescue and ferry across all sentient beings everywhere;
those whom you reach and deliver are established on the shore of Dharma without a moment's delay.
Having thus crossed over the entire multitude of sentient beings, they are as numerous as the sands within the waters of the great ocean.
Having emerged, he immediately reveals the true path; within the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing superior—do not harbor doubt.
The Buddha can grasp the bell of that Dharma and cause all beings everywhere to know and hear it.
By the power transmitted through the ringing of that bell, the ocean of afflictions is entirely extinguished.
Just as when the radiant form of the sun appears, The darkness that obscures the eyes is entirely dispelled;
So too for those ignorant and witless people, Their afflictions are extinguished and the light of wisdom becomes pure.
When ignorance and afflictions shroud the eyes, All manner of defilements follow along with them.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, He causes them all, in due order, to attain purity.
Manifesting spiritual transformations according to the needs of beings, Like the bright moon appearing in water;
Yet to those of false wisdom, the blind from birth, and evil beings, The Buddha does not appear before their very eyes.
Just as hungry ghosts standing on the shore of the great ocean See all the waters of the sea as completely parched,
So too do these beings of meager merit and evil nature Constantly say with their own mouths,
"There is no Buddha. Such classes of beings of meager merit— Even the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot save them.
Just as one born blind, a person without sight, Does not see a bright jewel held before them, Who has the power to enable them to behold it? So too is the stainless, pure, and wondrous Dharmakāya;
Like the radiance of ten billion suns, Enveloped by a web of flames, it cannot be seen.
Just as the gods with meager merit cannot see even ordinary beings of the lower realms, how much less can they see the body of the Great Lord Maheśvara?
How could the ignorant and deluded masses ever perceive the form and countenance of that Great Lord Maheśvara?
Even seers possessing the five supernatural powers do not see him.
How much more so for the eight classes of non-human spirits and wicked sentient beings—

only by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power can they see it. Those who practice the yoga of contemplation to purify their minds and bestow happiness upon all sentient beings, being wise and discerning, will indeed be able to see it.
If there are sentient beings possessing merit, they will always perceive all Buddhas before them, adorned by the surrounding halo of light;
furthermore, they shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
If one knows such great diligence, one can behold the ocean of wisdom, profound and vast.
These sentient beings shall before long possess merit as vast as the great ocean;
if they can listen to this sublime verse, they will practice it themselves and attain vision.
Upon passing away, they will be born within a great lotus flower and be able to hear the Buddhas preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha,
having spoken these verses,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He returned to his original seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you have been able to skillfully speak these sublime verses.
If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, maintain mindfulness of, and contemplate this,
that person shall immediately attain the peerless Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas,
as well as the unforgetting secret treasury of the Tathāgatas’ wisdom.
Therefore, one does not remain long within the three realms,
but immediately attains liberation. Having attained liberation for oneself, [one liberates others].
He also causes all sentient beings to attain liberation.
He enables those who hear him to practice according to his teachings.
While he was speaking these words, [the earth shook].
Immeasurable devas and humans entered the path of the One Vehicle,
and there were also immeasurable bodhisattvas from other directions.
He attained the ultimate stage of non-retrogression.
Chapter Three: The Inquiry of the Bodhisattva Sadāpradāna. At that time, there was a bodhisattva within the assembly.
Named Constantly Bestowing,
he rose from his seat, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
and bared one shoulder.
Placing his right knee on the ground and joining his palms toward the Buddha,
he addressed the Buddha, saying:
I now have a slight doubt and venture to consult you about it;
I fear my request may be a source of disturbance.
I fear it may offend the Holy One’s mind;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will not hold this as a fault.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing:
"The Tathāgata has already transcended the eight worldly dharmas."
"Ask whatever you wish;
why need you have any doubt?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing (Nityapradāna) [spoke].
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
after one thousand five hundred years have passed since the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa..."
All inferior sentient beings will no longer behold the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgata,
nor shall they hear the true flavor of the meaning of the Dharma.
When the True Dharma is extinguished and the Semblance Dharma comes to an end,
the evil hearts and malicious intentions of sentient beings will blaze forth with intensity.
There is no time that is not real.
At that time, if sentient beings are to be disciplined, [it occurs].
What Dharma do you teach?
How do you abide? How do you practice?
What kind of meritorious deed is most excellent for ensuring that one does not fall into the evil realms?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will,
out of compassion, explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
He addressed the Bodhisattva Nityadatta, saying:
"Alas, alas! The sentient beings of the future!"
They possess not the slightest compassion and repeatedly commit evil deeds. Why is this?
At that time, because of the power of ignorance and darkness, all sentient beings—
Unaware of one's own benefit,
one accumulates merit as vast as Mount Sumeru,
yet the reward obtained is exceedingly small.
Good son, in future ages, all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and upāsakas—
Upāsikā, king, prince.
Ministers, officials, and brahmins.
The householder,
Vatsa, Śreṣṭhara, and so forth.
Within the discipline of my teachings and laws,
they lack a heart of respect toward the Three Jewels.
They lack a mind of reverence;
they possess not even a fraction of the true meaning of the Dharma;
nor do they perform any wholesome deeds whatsoever on its account.
Because they single-mindedly seek fame, profit, and victory over others,
not for a single moment do they give rise to the mind of world-transcendence.
Furthermore, good son:
In future ages, during the period of the Semblance Dharma,
there will be immeasurable evil matters.
Evil deeds increase further.
What are these evil matters? What are they?
All monastics and laypeople alike do not recognize the rules of the Dharma and do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
All worldly people lack skillful means;
when worldly people hold assemblies to seek merit, [they do so without such means].
Please summon the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
for fear that too many might come,
one might give rise to a mind of stinginess and attachment.
Even if one dispatches people to guard the gates and watch over the doors,
those who are not known to them [will not be admitted].
Do not allow entry for those who are poor beggars or those who are old and sick.
They were likewise not permitted to enter.
Thus, when the assembly was convened in this manner,
the disciples lost the food and drink.
There is no portion of merit whatsoever;
rather, it invites sinful karma because of the practice of unequal giving.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who,
with a single-minded focus on their own benefit,
long for merit and virtue.
They do not act for the benefit of others;
they do not accept the teachings of others;
and when they see others practicing merit, [they do not rejoice].
They cannot rejoice in it,
nor can they assist even a small portion of it,
O son of good family.
You should know that such sentient beings possess not even the slightest merit.
Furthermore, good son, in a future age,
there will again be various sentient beings.
Seeing that others’ former ruined stupas, ruined temples, ruined scriptures, and ruined images were dilapidated and destroyed,
they had no intention to repair them.
Yet when someone urged them to do so, [they would comply].
And he spoke these words:
"This was not created by my own school or its followers;
what use is there in practicing it?"
"Why not simply create a new one for me yourself?
Why rely on repairing the old?
"Good son," [the Buddha replied].
You should know this: when repairing what is old,
one must not create anything new.
Regarding fundamental merit,
one further attains superior blessings;
this is because of those who create and establish [the image] anew.
It is not as good as cultivating the immeasurable and boundless merit of the past.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who see many others gathered together in one place.
They perform various meritorious deeds and each practice giving according to their own capacity and means.
When they see others giving to them, [they rejoice].
Out of envy, jealousy, and pride,
for the sake of fame and reputation,
he squandered all the wealth and property within his own household.
If one gives alms in such a manner,
that person will obtain very little merit.
Why is this? Because their minds are callous and they lack compassion.
Furthermore, upon seeing those who are poor, solitary, distressed,
or beggars, he reviles, pushes aside, and drives them away,
forcing them out through the gates.
Without giving away even a single thing,
such sentient beings are said to perform merit through perversion.
This is called performing merit while deluded and insane;
it is also called performing merit improperly.
Such is this wholesome karma.
Transmigrating through the various realms of existence,
those people [behave] toward those who are hungry and poor.
One must arouse compassion.
Even if one possesses abundant wealth, gold, silver, ornaments, clothing, food, drink, beds, couches, and bedding—
such things as these should be given as gifts.
Do not worry about poverty;
yet when wealth is expended in great abundance,
the blessings obtained are very few.
"You should know this.
Furthermore, son of good family,
at one time, in various sūtras, I [taught]..."
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
If there are sentient beings who lack skillful means, [he teaches them accordingly].

Those devoid of compassion have practiced various forms of giving for incalculable eons before the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as before bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even their own bodies.
By means of this practice of giving for the sake of making offerings,
that person’s merit [is as follows].
"Would it not be much?
It would be very much,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha told Nityadatta:
"Suppose there were a person who possessed compassion."
The merit of this person who, with a heart of respect and through skillful means, gives even a single morsel of food to an animal.
It surpasses the previous merit by hundreds of thousands of millions of times,
being incalculable and boundless.
Why is this? Because with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion,
they delight in giving.
Because one attains great fruit;
because that food is difficult to obtain;
and because there is no expectation of reward.
Furthermore, son of good family,
I have taught the practice of giving in various sūtras in order to guide both householders and those who have left the home life.
Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
Practice giving to those who are poor, orphaned, aged,
or afflicted by malignant diseases and grave illnesses.
Even when beset by suffering, distress, and calamity, down to the point of being like dogs,
they constantly practice giving;
in future lives, [they shall attain...]
My disciples do not understand my intention; they devote themselves exclusively to making offerings to the field of merit.
Regarding the field of compassion and the field of reverence:
the field of reverence refers to the Three Jewels.
The field of compassion refers to those who are poor, orphaned, elderly, and so forth, down to even the smallest ants. Why is this?
In future ages, between these two kinds of fields,
the field of compassion is the most supreme.
Furthermore, good son,
if there is a person of wealth and status who possesses abundant riches and goods.
He practiced giving alone,
from the age of twelve until he was one hundred years old.
I say that one makes offerings to the Triple Gem for the sake of seeking fame and reputation.
The merit of this person is very slight.
It is not as good as that of many people who, with one mind— regardless of whether they are poor or wealthy, noble or humble, lay or ordained—
exhort and transform one another together.
Whether many or few,
each according to their own capacity,
shall relinquish a small amount of wealth and goods.
Gathering together in one place,
they maintained an uninterrupted succession,
bestowing gifts upon all who were poor, orphaned, and aged.
I speak of those with malignant diseases and grave illnesses,
and those in distress who are fields of compassion.
This person possesses the greatest merit;
even if they do not practice giving,
within every moment of thought, [they possess it].
The merit produced through such effort is constant and inexhaustible.
If there are those with faith who rejoice in this,
[the merit shall likewise be boundless].
The merit obtained by such a person is likewise thus,
even when practicing giving alone.
That merit will be very slight.
Furthermore, good son, in a future age...
My disciples delight in fine clothing and delight in fine food and drink.
They delight in seeking gain and offerings;
because they are shrouded by delusion and craving,
they are stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous.
A vast accumulation of various kinds of wealth and goods within the field of compassion.
They lack any intention to give,
do not cultivate loving-kindness and compassion,
and are exclusively given to anger and resentment.
Seeing others performing meritorious deeds,
they scrutinized them with contempt and disparagement, all saying:
This person maintains a wrong livelihood through flattery and crookedness,
seeking fame and profit;
if he sees a poor beggar, [he treats them with contempt].
They treat others with contempt and mockery;
seeing someone else being given a gift,
they again deride and laugh at them.
They speak of their faults and evils,
and together they utter words of slander against those who have left the household life.
"What is the use of giving?
Thus spoke the Buddha to the ordained bhikṣus.
One should practice two types of conduct:
first, recitation and study;
second, meditative concentration.
Furthermore, since you have studied and possess much learning and wisdom,
what use is there for the distracting business of giving? Good son!
If one lacks a heart of compassion toward sentient beings,
one departs from the path of the Buddha.
It is exceedingly remote.
Therefore, son of good family,
you should know this.
Such a person is a member of Māra’s retinue.
If there are those who perform good deeds and cultivate merit, [they will be opposed by them].
Whether they be monastics or laypeople,
those who speak of such people's faults and evils—
such persons [are as follows].
After the end of their life,
they fall into the great hells,
where their lifespan is exceedingly long.
They undergo suffering in the hells for many kalpas; after dying from the hells,
they fall among the hungry ghosts.
The head is like Mount Tai;
the throat is like the eye of a needle;
the belly is like the great ocean.
After twelve years had passed,
they did not even hear the name of water, let alone see it.
They suffered from great hunger;
having emerged from the realm of hungry ghosts,
they remained there for five hundred lifetimes.
They fall among the animals;
having emerged from the animal realm,
for five hundred lifetimes...
Born into a poor and lowly family,
they constantly undergo suffering and affliction,
without a single moment of mental ease.
Why is this? Because when seeing others give,
one does not rejoice in it.
Because they seek out the faults of others.
Furthermore, son of good family,
throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I...
For the sake of all sentient beings who suffer from poverty,
I have exhorted one another to gather goods together in one place.
By practicing such giving,
one will, through these causes and conditions,
swiftly attain Buddhahood.
And as for the Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions,
they too have likewise come forth from giving.
And thus one attains Buddhahood. Within all the sūtras,
I have expounded upon the various pāramitās.
All of these take generosity as their primary foundation,
O son of good family.
For example, suppose there is a person whose two feet are both broken;
though he intends to travel far to reach a place of jewels,
can this person go far?
"Is it not that what is sought is not obtained? "No,
World-Honored One."
For what reason?
Because they are without feet,
World-Honored One.
He said: "That person is also like this regarding the five pāramitās."
Seeking maturation,
they do not practice giving even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In the end, one will be unable to reach the further shore of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
If one does not practice giving.
Then there would be no precepts;
if there were no precepts,
then there would be no compassionate mind.
If there is no compassion,
then there is no loving-kindness.
If there is no loving-kindness...
Then one cannot endure.
If there is no patience,
then there is no diligence.
If there is no diligence,
then there is no meditative concentration; if there is no meditative concentration, [there is no wisdom].
Then there is no wisdom.
Because there is no wisdom,
one is constantly susceptible to the influence of immeasurable adventitious afflictions.
Good son, it is for this reason that this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
This Dharma gate of giving is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time collectively revere.
Furthermore, they transform sentient beings,
causing them to respect and practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
For this reason, among the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu):
"Gathering through material wealth is the most excellent.
Son of good family,
at one time or another, I..."
I praise the observance of ethical discipline; at other times,
I praise patience.
At times I praise diligence; at other times I...
I praise meditative concentration; at other times, I praise wisdom.
At times I praise the dhūta practices;
at other times I [do not].
He praised having few desires and being content; or at other times,
he praised the śrāvakas.
Or again, at one time he praised the pratyekabuddhas;
or again, at another time.
They praise the Bodhisattvas in these various ways,
according to the differing capacities of sentient beings.
Good son, in future ages there will be much sinful karma.
The bhikṣus did not understand my intention;
each clung to their own views and mutually criticized one another as being right or wrong.
They do not practice my Dharma. For this reason,
they cause my teaching to become inverted and confused.
That which is truly the Buddha-dharma is spoken of as non-Dharma; that which is truly not the Buddha-dharma [is spoken of as such].
This is called the Buddha-dharma.
Because it is spoken thus,
this true dharma of mine [is established].
They will then be destroyed;
only a small portion of similar qualities will remain in those evil bhikṣus.
He spoke thus: "The Semblance Dharma shall also perish.
Once the Semblance Dharma has perished,"
The teachings have all come to an end. Good son,
such is the bhikṣu.
They are unable to understand my profound meaning,
nor do they understand my skillful means and wisdom; furthermore,
they do not know the proper time.
Ascending the lion throne,
he naturally lost his majestic deportment as he preached the Dharma for others.
To grasp the meaning only according to the literal text,
without grasping the true intent,
is to contradict the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
He constantly praised himself, saying:
"What I have now spoken is no different from that of the Buddha."
As for the other Dharma masters,
they were unacquainted with the meaning of the Dharma and deceived both monastics and laypeople.
Seeing their own superiority,
they act within the great assembly for the sake of fame and profit.
He constantly praises his own virtues,
O son of good family.
Such is the bhikṣu.
Those who speak such words shall fall into the great hells and undergo all manner of suffering.
Emerging from hell,
they transmigrate through birth and death.
Furthermore, son of good family:
Various wicked bhikṣus,
seeing others sitting in meditation,
gave rise to contempt and disparagement.
They discussed it in detail together, saying:
"This man is foolish;
what could he possibly have studied?"
It is merely idleness;
what meditative concentration could there be?
One falsely manifests the signs of dhyāna.
They deceive others; they do not listen to the sūtras or śāstras,
and they possess no knowledge or understanding.
How could such a person be able to practice seated meditation?
O son of good family,
such a person as this—
Those who speak such words will suffer for many kalpas,
with no time of escape.
Furthermore, son of good family,
such evil bhikṣus, for the sake of fame and profit, [act in this way].
They will engage in mutual criticism and contention,
thereby destroying my true Dharma and Vinaya,
and they will no longer rely on their teachers for study.
They practice meditation within their own minds,
clinging to their own views and taking what is wrong for what is right.
Unable to distinguish between what is heterodox and what is orthodox,
he constantly spoke these words to both monastics and laypeople.
I understand the methods of dhyāna;
I am able to know reality;
I am able to see this.
Good son, such a person extinguishes my eye of Dharma.
They fall into hell themselves.
Furthermore, good son, my evil disciples—
He says of himself, "I understand the Sūtras and Vinaya," yet he does not actually understand them;
he himself violates the precepts.
Being unable to comprehend my true meaning,
they speak thus:
"In the Vinaya taught by the Blessed One..."
I have permitted the eating of meat.
Good son, if I were to explain the faults of eating meat, [it would be as follows].
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and bodhisattvas of the first stage have their minds utterly bewildered and distressed.
Having no understanding,
they harbor feelings of sorrow and suffering. Good son!
Such persons as these falsely slander me,
O son of good family.
In the Vinaya, for the sake of those who are ill,
it is permitted to eat the three kinds of pure meat.
All of these are inconceivable;
you should know this,
O son of good family.
From the time I attained Buddhahood until this very day,
my śrāvaka disciples—
Whenever ordinary beings see those who consume meat in various places having finished their meal, they [perceive it as such].
They form this thought:
"I truly see him eating meat;
he does not know that I possess skillful means."
To speak erroneously and with perversion is to incur a grave and heavy offense.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings...
When he saw various sick bhikṣus eating meat,
he entered deeply into the Dharma-gate of immeasurable wisdom;
furthermore, there were immeasurable witnesses.
They sever the afflictions of the lower realm,
they sever the afflictions of the upper realm,
and they sever the afflictions of the middle realm.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who deliver sentient beings and cause them to transcend birth and death.
They enter the path of the Tathāgata and attain the further shore. Why is this?
Good son, this is the Tathāgata’s teaching and preaching of the Dharma.
It is inconceivable. You should know this, for it is for the sake of taming all sentient beings.
My śrāvaka disciples have never eaten the flesh of sentient beings;
how much less so, then, the bodhisattvas?
In the Vinaya, for the sake of sick bhikṣus, I have followed the conventions of worldly physicians.
Regarding those who must eat the three kinds of pure meat:
what kind of meat is this?
Good son, [it is as follows].
You should know that those meats do not arise from the four great elements;
they are not born from a womb, nor born from an egg, nor born from moisture,
nor born through transformation.
It does not unite with consciousness;
it does not unite with life-force.
It is neither real nor unreal.
You should know that in the world there is no such meat at all;
this was spoken by me as a skillful means.
They do not understand my intention and thus harm their own bodies.
Furthermore, good son:
In future ages, there will be many wicked bhikṣus in every kingdom,
every city, every village, and every monastery, in all such places.
They lecture on the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras,
grasping the meaning according to the literal text,
yet failing to comprehend the profound and secret essential teachings of the Tathāgata.
"Good son, when I appeared in the world,
I preached to the great assembly that one may eat the flesh of sentient beings."
This is impossible.
One who eats meat possesses no compassion.
Those who lack compassion are not my disciples;
I am not their teacher.
Why is this? Because within this great assembly,
each possesses a different nature.
Each has different views;
how much more so will those of future generations? Good son!
Within this assembly now,
some see the Tathāgata remaining in the world for an eon,
while others see the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa.
Some may be born and yet not see me at all;
others may see my body.
Sometimes they do not see my body;
sometimes they see my body as being twice as tall as three men;
or they see the Tathāgata’s body of radiant light.
Some see him with a vast body; some see him as a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);
and some see him as the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) seated upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury World.
Surrounded by bodhisattvas,
he dwells within an ocean of immeasurable worlds,
preaching the Dharma in accordance with the minds of the great assembly.
Or there are those who see my Dharma-body as being identical to empty space:
devoid of form or appearance,
and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Pure and unobstructed.
Some may see me dwelling between the twin śāla trees,
while others do not see me.
Some see this ground as consisting of earth, sand, gravel, and stones;
others, deluded, see this ground surrounded on all sides by various forests, earthen mounds, and stone walls;
or they see this ground and the walls and so forth as being composed entirely of the seven treasures.

Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās,
devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
Gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas.
Kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
they prostrated at his feet and their hearts were filled with great joy.
They received and practiced it with faith.
Each person prepared the implements for the cremation,
their grief moving both heaven and earth.

*The Sūtra on the Mirror of Yoga Dharma Revealing Transgressions Spoken by the Buddha*, one fascicle. On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of the year Jǐwǔ (the Year of the Horse) in the first year of the Jǐnglóng era, the Tripiṭaka Master Śrīmitra (translated into Chinese as Miàohuì) translated this at Chóngfú Monastery. The Great Virtuous Monk and Sramana Śīla of Dàxīngshàn Monastery received the oral transmission and compiled the text; the Great Virtuous Monk and Sramana Dà'ān of Dàcí'ēn Monastery and others verified the meaning. The Chief Official Ān Dàmó served as the interpreter. On the thirteenth day of the third month in the second year of the Jǐngyún era, it was submitted for promulgation.
